data.title: DOM
data.tagline: The DOM is the node tree the browser uses to represent and modify a web document.
data.learningOutcome: You can inspect the runtime DOM and script when the current page differs from initial HTML, and distinguish a page update from persisted data.
data.description: For example, the source HTML may contain one task while a click adds another to the page. A script created a node and inserted it into the runtime DOM. That change affects the current page, but whether it survives a refresh depends on separate persistence in a backend or browser storage.

learning.assumes: You have seen page source and encountered new content or elements appearing after a click.
learning.outcome: You can inspect the runtime DOM and script when the current page differs from initial HTML, and distinguish a page update from persisted data.

distinctions.label: HTML
distinctions.explanation: HTML is the document source that describes the initial structure; DOM is the browser's current node tree after parsing and runtime changes.

distinctions.label: Browser storage
distinctions.explanation: DOM changes what the current page shows; Browser Storage is a separate mechanism for keeping data in the browser across page loads.

explanation.title: The browser parses the document first
explanation.text: The browser reads HTML and organizes its elements, text, and attributes into a hierarchy of nodes that begins the page render.

explanation.title: A script can change the tree
explanation.text: After a click, JavaScript can create, remove, or change nodes, so the DOM in Elements may differ from the original HTML file.

data.boundary: The DOM is the browser's current runtime document tree, not the initial HTML file and not a database. A task inserted into the DOM may disappear on refresh; retaining it across refreshes, devices, or users requires separate data storage. Modern frontend frameworks (like React or Vue) help manage DOM updates—you describe what the interface should look like, and the framework automatically calculates which nodes need to change. AI-generated React code rarely uses `document.createElement`, because the framework manipulates this tree behind the scenes for you.

lessonPractice.title: A task appears after clicking Add, but it is missing from View Source. What should you determine next?

options.label: Inspect the runtime DOM and script to see how the new node was created and inserted
options.feedback: Correct. View Source shows the initial document; the runtime DOM in Elements shows the node change after the click.

options.label: Write the task into the initial HTML so it is visible from the start
options.feedback: That turns click-generated content into fixed content and still does not explain how the script updates the current page.

options.label: Treat the new task as saved data and inspect the database record directly
options.feedback: A DOM update proves only that the current page has a node. It does not prove a database write; refresh persistence needs a separate check.

data.agentPrompt: After clicking Add, inspect whether the runtime DOM contains the new task node and identify which script inserted it. Then refresh to determine whether this was only a DOM update or was persisted. Do not treat a visible node as proof of a database write.
